Growing the Integration Suite

Comment and Tag get their own supertest files; Ticket's grows to cover every new route this lesson added.

The integration-testing approach itself doesn't change from Lesson 2: mock db.js with jest.unstable_mockModule before importing app.js (Figure 2.20), then drive real routes through it with supertest — no database, but real Express routing and middleware, validate.js included. What's new this lesson is scale: tickets.routes.test.js grows to cover PATCH/DELETE and the filtering/pagination query string, and two new files — comments.routes.test.js, tags.routes.test.js — apply the same pattern to this lesson's other two resources.

// Figure 3.17: the same mocked-app pattern, applied to a nested resource (tests/integration/comments.routes.test.js, excerpt)
it('PATCH .../comments/:id 404s when the comment is on a different ticket', async () => {
  mockPrisma.comment.findFirst.mockResolvedValue(null);

  const res = await request(app).patch('/tickets/1/comments/9').send({ body: 'Edited' });

  expect(res.status).toBe(404);
  expect(mockPrisma.comment.update).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
});

This one exercises the scoped-lookup behavior from the nested-routes topic directly: mocking comment.findFirst to resolve null simulates exactly the case where a comment exists but belongs to a different ticket than the URL names, and the test asserts both halves of the correct outcome — a 404 reaches the client, and comment.update is never even attempted.

Between the validator tests, the middleware test, and this growing integration suite, the project now tests the same behavior at three different levels — a schema in isolation, one piece of middleware in isolation, and a full request through real routing — each catching a different kind of mistake, and each cheap enough to keep writing as more routes are added in the weeks ahead.
